summary: Defines the string form used in LDAP for distinguished names, the keys that identify entries in an X.500 directory. It reads cleanly for common names but can still represent any distinguished name. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: How to write down the full address of a directory entry as plain text, like country, then company, then person.

subtitle: How LDAP writes a directory entry's full name as a plain UTF-8 string, such as UID=jsmith,DC=example,DC=net.

tldr.problem: X.500 directories identify every entry by a distinguished name (DN) that is defined as an ASN.1 structure, but LDAP needs a text form that is easy to encode and decode.
tldr.mechanism: A DN is written as a comma-separated list of relative names, written last element first. Each is a type=value pair, with a small set of escape rules for special characters and a hex form for anything else.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4514 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2253. It does not define a canonical form, so DNs are compared with the distinguishedNameMatch matching rule.

facts.value: 9 (CN, L, ST, O, OU, C, STREET, DC, UID)

sections.title: Why DNs Need a String Form
sections.content:
In X.500-based directories, including those reached with LDAP, distinguished names (DNs) are the primary keys that unambiguously refer to directory entries. Their structure is described in ASN.1. In the X.500 Directory Access Protocol, DNs are encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER). In LDAP, they are carried in the string form this RFC defines.

The primary goal is ease of encoding and decoding. A secondary goal is human readability. The RFC does not expect LDAP user interfaces to show these strings directly; it expects them to translate, for example by showing attribute type names in the local national language.

The RFC does not define a canonical string form. DNs are compared for equality with the distinguishedNameMatch matching rule from RFC 4517, not by comparing strings.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers need a way to write down exactly which entry in a big phone book you mean. This RFC says how to write that address as simple text.

sections.title: Turning a DN into a String
sections.content:
The RFC gives a RECOMMENDED algorithm. A DN is a sequence of relative distinguished names (RDNs). The output lists the RDNs starting from the last element of the sequence and moving backwards, separated by a comma. An empty sequence becomes the empty string.

An RDN may hold several attribute type and value pairs. They are written in any order and joined with a plus sign (+). Each pair is the attribute type, an equals sign, and the value.

The attribute type is written as its registered short name (a descriptor such as CN) when one is known. Otherwise it is written as the dotted-decimal form of its OBJECT IDENTIFIER. Implementations SHOULD provide a way to update their knowledge of registered short names.

When the type is dotted-decimal, or the value's syntax has no suitable UTF-8 string form, the value is written as a number sign followed by the hex of its BER encoding. Otherwise the value is a UTF-8 string, and some characters must be escaped: a leading space or number sign, a trailing space, any of " + , ; < > \, and the null character. An escape is a backslash and two hex digits, or, for a few characters, a backslash in front of the character itself.
sections.plainLanguage: You list the parts of the address from the smallest to the biggest, separated by commas. If a name has a comma in it, you put a backslash in front so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: The Grammar and Required Names
sections.content:
Strings are restricted to UTF-8 Unicode and specified in ABNF. A distinguishedName is zero or more relativeDistinguishedName items separated by commas. Each RDN is one or more attributeTypeAndValue items separated by plus signs. A value is either a string or a hexstring.

To read a string value, each escape pair is replaced from left to right, without recursion: an escaped backslash becomes a backslash, an escaped special character becomes that character, and a backslash with a hex pair becomes the octet it names. A hexstring is converted back to BER octets pair by pair.

Implementations MUST recognize these descriptors, and MAY recognize others: CN, L, ST, O, OU, C, STREET, DC and UID. They are described in RFC 4519.

Implementations MAY recognize other DN string forms. Because that is not required, they SHOULD generate only strings that follow Section 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The grammar is the spelling rulebook. Anyone who follows it can read your address back correctly, and everyone must know the nine common labels such as CN for a name.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a few DNs. UID=jsmith,DC=example,DC=net has three RDNs. OU=Sales+CN=J. Smith,DC=example,DC=net has a multi-valued first RDN. CN=James \"Jim\" Smith\, III,DC=example,DC=net shows escaped quotes and comma. CN=Before\0dAfter,DC=example,DC=net shows a carriage return written as a hex escape.

An unrecognized type can be written with the BER hex form: 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.0=#04024869 is an OCTET STRING of the two octets 0x48 and 0x69. The last example is a commonName of five letters, where the two accented letters become UTF-8 octets written as hex escapes, giving printable ASCII CN=Lu\C4\8Di\C4\87, which is useful for debugging.
sections.plainLanguage: Here are sample addresses showing each trick: commas inside names, a name with two parts, and letters with accents turned into safe codes.

sections.title: Disclosure and Reversibility
sections.content:
DNs usually hold descriptive information about the thing they name, such as a person's full name, an email or TCP/IP address, a physical location or an organizational attribute. Some of this can be sensitive, and privacy laws in many countries restrict disclosing some of it. Server implementers are encouraged to support DIT structural rules and name forms, and administrators to use access controls to keep sensitive attributes out of entry names.

The string conversion is not always reversible. A commonName of Sam as a TeletexString and one as a PrintableString both become CN=Sam. Applications that need the DER form, such as when verifying an X.509 certificate, SHOULD NOT use the string forms of attribute syntaxes. They SHOULD use the number-sign hex form instead.
sections.plainLanguage: An address can give away private things like where someone works. Also, two different original spellings can look the same in text, so if you need the exact original, use the safe hex code.

sections.title: Presentation and Changes Since RFC 2253
sections.content:
Appendix A is informational. It advises that user interfaces use hex pair escaping for non-printable characters. It also notes that < and > must be escaped inside a DN, so they can wrap a DN in free text, as in <CN=Sam\ >. Long DNs can be line-wrapped, but the RFC says inserting whitespace is not advised. LDIF is offered as an alternative.

Appendix B lists changes from RFC 2253. Highlights: any registered short name may now appear instead of a fixed table, the table moved to Section 3, alternative string forms are allowed, hex escaping applies to all characters, the null character must be escaped, ABNF from RFC 4234 replaced the old grammar, and LDAPv2-only requirements were removed because LDAPv2 is Historic.
sections.plainLanguage: The back of the RFC gives tips on showing addresses to people and lists what changed from the older version.
